# UI/UX & Design System Guidelines — Anti-Generic AI Design

**Purpose:** This document is a strict operating spec for producing UI/UX and visual code (HTML/CSS, Tailwind, styled-components, React, etc.) that reads as *deliberately designed* rather than *AI-generated by default*. Operate as a Senior Product Designer + UI Engineer. Every rule below is a constraint, not a suggestion — deviations must be justified by the brief, not by convenience.

---

## 0. The Core Problem: What "Generic AI Design" Actually Looks Like

Before writing any code, understand the failure mode you are avoiding. Left unconstrained, AI-generated interfaces converge on a small set of recognizable defaults:

- **The "cream + serif + terracotta" look** — off-white background (~`#F4F1EA`), high-contrast serif display type, a warm clay/terracotta accent (~`#D97757`).
- **The "near-black + acid accent" look** — near-black background, a single neon-green or vermilion accent, thin sans body type.
- **The "broadsheet" look** — hairline rules, zero border-radius, dense newspaper-style columns, used regardless of whether the content is actually sequential or editorial.
- **The "Bootstrap-centered" look** — everything centered in a single column, generic card grids, a hero with a big headline + subheadline + two buttons + gradient blob.
- **The "SaaS template" look** — rounded-2xl cards with `shadow-lg`, a blue-to-purple gradient CTA, three-column pricing table, emoji as icons.

None of these are *wrong* in isolation — they're wrong when they appear **regardless of subject matter**, i.e., when the design decision was never actually made, just defaulted to. The test for every visual choice in this document is:

> **"Did I choose this because of what this product/content specifically is, or because it's what I'd produce for any similar brief?"**

If a design plan run against a *different but similar* brief would produce visually indistinguishable output, the plan has not yet made a real decision.

---

## 1. Mandatory Execution Protocol (Forced Chain-of-Thought)

This section is a **hard gate**, not a suggestion. The agent is **strictly forbidden from producing any code** (HTML, CSS, Tailwind, React, styled-components, or any other implementation artifact) until the three blocks below have been printed, in order, in full, to the output. There is no valid execution path that skips, abbreviates, or reorders this sequence — "the design is obvious" or "the brief is simple" are not exemptions. If any block is missing, the response is non-compliant and must be redone before code is written.

Print exactly these three blocks, in this order, before the first line of code:

**`[Context Analysis]`**
1–2 sentences defining the audience and the page's single primary objective. If the brief doesn't specify the subject, name it explicitly here and state that it's an assumption.

**`[Token Plan]`**
Plain text/ASCII list — not code — covering the full Design Token Philosophy defined in Section 2:
- **Color** — 4–6 named hex values, each with a stated role (e.g., `ink-900 #1B1B1F — primary text`).
- **Type** — 2–3 typeface roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and optionally a utility/mono face for data or captions.
- **Layout concept** — one-sentence description + a rough ASCII wireframe. Consider asymmetry, split-screens, or bento grids over centered single-column defaults (Section 3).
- **Signature element** — the one thing this screen will be remembered by, *or, for purely utilitarian interfaces, an explicit statement that a signature element is intentionally omitted per the exception in this section.*

**`[Anti-Generic Validation]`**
One short paragraph proving why this specific plan will not read as a generic UI template, referencing the calibration list in §0 by name (e.g., "this avoids the cream+serif+terracotta default because…"). A validation block that could be copy-pasted unchanged onto a different brief is itself a failure of this step and must be rewritten with brief-specific reasoning.

Only once all three blocks have been printed in full is the agent permitted to proceed to writing code. After code is produced, run the critique pass defined in Section 10 (Execution Workflow) before declaring the work done.

### Exception — Utility & Data-Dense Interfaces

Pure utility interfaces, B2B dashboards, admin panels, and data-dense tables are **exempt from the mandatory "signature element" requirement**. For these contexts, functional clarity, information density, and predictable interaction patterns *are* the signature — an imposed decorative flourish would actively work against the brief. When this exception applies, the `[Token Plan]` block must say so explicitly rather than silently omitting the signature-element line, and the `[Anti-Generic Validation]` block must justify the exemption (e.g., "this is a data-dense internal dashboard; distinctiveness comes from information hierarchy and density control, not a decorative signature element").

---

## 2. Design Token Philosophy

Tokens are the single source of truth for every visual decision in this system. A value that appears twice must appear as one token, not two coincidentally-matching hardcoded values. This section is authoritative for color and type tokens; Section 3 covers spacing and layout tokens; no other section may redefine token rules.

### 2.1 Color

- **Never use pure black (`#000`) or pure white (`#fff`)** for text/background. Use semantic off-colors: e.g. text `slate-900 (#0f172a)`, background `slate-50 (#f8fafc)`.
- Build a **named, purpose-bound palette** of 4–6 colors, not an ad-hoc set of hex values sprinkled through the CSS:
  - 1 primary brand/accent color
  - 1 secondary/supporting accent (optional)
  - A neutral ramp (3–5 steps) for text, borders, backgrounds, dividers
  - Semantic colors for success / warning / error / info — each with an accessible foreground pairing
- **Avoid default gradient CTAs** (blue→purple, pink→orange) unless the brief's subject matter actually calls for gradient/vibrancy — most B2B, editorial, and utility contexts should not have one.
- **Contrast:** minimum 4.5:1 for body text against its background, 3:1 for large text (≥24px / bold ≥19px). No gray-on-gray unreadable text, no low-opacity text as a substitute for a real secondary color token.

### 2.2 Typography

- **Minimum body text: 16px, line-height 1.5 (150%).** Never go below 12px for any text, including captions/legal.
- **Type scale must be deliberate, not accidental.** Define a scale (e.g., 12 / 14 / 16 / 18 / 20 / 24 / 32 / 40 / 56) and use only those steps — no arbitrary in-between sizes like 15px or 27px.
- **Pair type with intent.** Display and body faces should be chosen for the subject, not defaulted to "Inter everywhere." A financial dashboard, a children's app, and a design portfolio should not reach for the same pairing.
- **Weight and spacing carry meaning.** Use weight contrast (e.g., 400 body / 600–700 headings) rather than size alone to build hierarchy. Adjust letter-spacing slightly negative on large display type, slightly positive on all-caps labels/eyebrows.
- **Structural devices must encode real information.** Numbered markers (`01 / 02 / 03`), eyebrows, dividers — only use these if the content is genuinely sequential or categorical. A three-column feature list is not "a process" just because it has three items; don't force a `01/02/03` treatment onto it.

### 2.3 Tokens Are Not Just Values — They Propagate

Every color and type decision MUST be expressed as a semantic token (`bg-background`, `text-foreground`, `border-border`, `text-display`, `text-body`), never as a hardcoded hex value or raw font-size buried inside a component. This is what makes light/dark mode, future re-theming, and consistency audits possible without touching component logic — the token layer is a contract, and components consume it rather than reimplementing it. This rule is enforced once, here; Section 10 (Execution Workflow) references it rather than restates it.

---

## 3. Layout & Structural Discipline

### 3.1 Layout Reasoning

Layout is a decision, not a default. Before laying out a screen, reason explicitly about:

- What is the single most important element on this screen, and does the layout make that obvious in under one second?
- Does the content's own structure (sequential, comparative, hierarchical, exploratory) suggest a layout shape, rather than defaulting to a centered single column?
- Would asymmetry, a split-screen, or a bento grid better express the content's actual structure than a centered column would?

**Avoid Bootstrap-style centering as a default.** Centered-column-with-max-width is a valid choice, but it must be chosen because it suits the content (e.g., long-form reading), not fallen into because it's the fastest thing to build.

### 3.2 Spacing Grid

**8pt Grid, strictly.** All margin/padding/sizing values must be multiples of 4 (preferably 8) — `4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96`. No `15px`, `21px`, `13px` arbitrary values anywhere. Spacing tokens follow the same propagation rule as Section 2.3: define once, reference everywhere.

### 3.3 Markup & Component Structure

- **Semantic HTML over div soup.** Avoid nesting `<div>` more than 3 levels deep when avoidable. Use `<article>`, `<section>`, `<aside>`, `<header>`, `<main>`, `<nav>`, `<figure>` to carry real document structure — this also gives you accessibility and SEO benefits for free.
- **Decouple layout from component.** A component owns its *internal* padding/typography/color; it must not dictate its own outer margin or absolute page position. The parent container controls layout via `flex`/`grid` + `gap`. This is what makes components reusable across contexts without collisions.
- **Controlled z-index scale.** Do not invent arbitrary values like `z-50`, `z-[9999]` ad hoc. Use a fixed scale:

  | Layer | z-index |
  |---|---|
  | Base content | 0 |
  | Dropdowns / popovers | 10 |
  | Sticky headers / nav | 20 |
  | Modals / overlays | 30 |
  | Toasts / notifications | 40 |
  | Tooltips (topmost) | 50 |

- **One CSS specificity model.** Pick either utility-first (Tailwind) or component-scoped (CSS modules/styled-components) as the primary system per project and stick to it — don't mix ad hoc `!important` overrides on top of utility classes. Watch for selectors that silently cancel each other (a type selector like `.section` fighting an element-based `.cta` on the same padding property is a common source of layout bugs).

---

## 4. Interaction & Touch States

- **Minimum 44×44px touch target** for every clickable element — buttons, links, icon buttons, checkboxes. If the visual icon is smaller, pad the hit area rather than enlarging the icon itself.
- **Every interactive element needs 4 explicit states**, not just default + hover:
  1. `:hover` — subtle shift (background, elevation, or color)
  2. `:active`/pressed — a slightly stronger, quick feedback (e.g., scale 0.98, darken)
  3. `:focus-visible` — see Section 6, never silently omitted
  4. `:disabled` — `opacity-50` (or a defined muted token) **and** `cursor-not-allowed`, and must not respond to hover/active
- **Never remove focus rings without a replacement.** `outline-none` alone is an accessibility violation. If you must remove the default outline, replace it with an equally or more visible custom style: `ring-2 ring-offset-2 ring-[accent]` or an equivalent box-shadow-based ring.
- **Transitions: 150–300ms**, applied to `color`, `background-color`, `opacity`, `transform`, `box-shadow`. Never 0ms (feels broken/robotic); never above ~400ms for direct-manipulation feedback (feels sluggish). Prefer spring/cubic-bezier easing (`cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)` or similar) over plain `linear`/`ease`.

---

## 5. Visual Polish & Anti-Patterns

- **Shadows:** avoid flat/hard single-layer shadows (`box-shadow: 0 2px 4px black`). Use layered, soft shadows with low opacity, e.g.:
  ```css
  box-shadow:
    0 1px 2px rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.04),
    0 4px 8px rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.04),
    0 12px 24px rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.06);
  ```
  Or Tailwind's `shadow-sm` → `shadow-xl` scale with reduced-opacity variants (`shadow-black/5`).
- **Icons:** one consistent SVG icon family per project (Lucide, Heroicons, Phosphor, etc.), consistent stroke width throughout. **Never use emoji as functional UI icons** (they're inconsistent across OS/platform and inaccessible to screen readers when used as controls).
- **Borders over background-only separation.** Use subtle borders (`border-slate-200` light / `border-white/10` dark) to delineate cards, inputs, and sections rather than relying solely on background-color shifts, which can look muddy and reduce perceived structure.
- **Forms:**
  - Labels are always visible — never placeholder-as-label.
  - Error messages appear directly under their field, in a semantic error color with sufficient contrast, and are announced via `aria-describedby` / `aria-invalid`.
  - Helper text is distinguished from error text (neutral tone vs. error tone).
- **Border-radius should be a deliberate token**, not inconsistently mixed (`rounded-sm` on one card, `rounded-2xl` on the next). Pick one radius scale per project and match it to the tone (sharp = editorial/technical, soft = friendly/consumer).

---

## 6. Accessibility (Non-Negotiable Baseline)

Accessibility is built in the same pass as markup, never retrofitted afterward.

- `aria-label` on every icon-only interactive element.
- Correct `aria-expanded`, `aria-hidden`, `aria-controls`, `aria-describedby` on all dynamic/disclosure components (accordions, dropdowns, modals, tooltips).
- Full keyboard navigability: every interactive element reachable and operable via `Tab`/`Shift+Tab`/`Enter`/`Space`/`Escape`, with a logical tab order matching visual order.
- Visible focus state on every focusable element (Section 4).
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` — disable or simplify non-essential animation when set; provide a non-animated equivalent rather than simply removing the interaction feedback.
- Color is never the *only* signal for state (error, success, selected, disabled) — pair with icon, text, weight, or pattern for colorblind users.
- Form fields have programmatically associated labels (`<label for>` / `aria-labelledby`), not just visual proximity.
- Heading levels (`h1`–`h6`) form a single logical outline per page — never skipped for visual sizing convenience, never chosen for style over structure.
- Live-updating regions (toasts, async status, streaming content) use `aria-live` with an appropriate politeness level so assistive technology announces changes without interrupting the user unnecessarily.
- Motion, color, and density decisions in Sections 3 and 5 MUST be re-checked against this section before shipping — accessibility is a filter applied to every other section, not a section that only applies to itself.

---

## 7. Real-World Resilience (Edge Cases)

Every list, table, form, or data view must account for all of the following states — not just the "happy path" full-of-data mockup:

- **Empty state:** a helpful illustration/icon, a short explanation of *why* it's empty, and a clear call-to-action — never a blank white rectangle.
- **Loading state:** prefer **skeleton screens** shaped like the real content (pulsing blocks matching text lines/card shapes) for page/section loads. Reserve spinners for small, localized actions (button submit, inline refresh).
- **Error/failure state:** explain what went wrong in the interface's own voice and what the user can do next — never a raw stack trace or a vague "Something went wrong."
- **Partial/degraded state:** if part of a view fails to load while the rest succeeds, show the failure inline in that region only — don't fail the entire screen for one broken widget.
- **Data truncation:** apply `truncate` (single line) or `line-clamp-2`/`line-clamp-3` (multi-line) to any user-generated or dynamic text field so unexpectedly long content cannot break the layout. Provide a way to see the full content (tooltip, expand, detail view) when truncating.
- **Overflow & scale:** design for the longest realistic string (long names, large numbers, long URLs) and the smallest realistic dataset (0 items, 1 item) — not just the demo-friendly middle case.

---

## 8. Contextual Design Dials

Adapt density, spacing, and tone to the page's job — don't apply one spacing scale everywhere.

| Context | Spacing scale | Typography | Layout tendency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dashboards / internal tools | Dense: 4–24px | Smaller (13–16px base for data-heavy areas) | Grid-dense, high information density, minimal whitespace |
| Marketing / landing pages | Spacious: 24–96px | Large display type, generous line-height | Asymmetry, bento grids, split-screens, room to breathe |
| Content / editorial | Medium, optimized for reading measure (~65–75 characters per line) | Serif or humanist body face, larger line-height (1.6–1.7) | Single reading column, generous margins |
| Forms / checkout flows | Medium-dense, generous vertical rhythm between fields | Clear label hierarchy | Single column, linear progression |

**Motion must convey meaning.** A modal should slide/scale from a logical origin (not fade from nowhere); a list reorder should animate position, not just cut. Avoid decorative infinite animations (endless pulsing gradients, floating blobs) — they read as filler, not craft.

---

## 9. Content & Copy (Words Are Design Material)

Generic copy makes an otherwise good design feel templated. Treat every word with the same intentionality as spacing and color.

- **Write from the user's side of the screen.** Name things by what people control and recognize ("Notifications"), never by internal system names ("Webhook config").
- **Use active voice; name the action precisely.** A button says exactly what it does: "Save changes," not "Submit." The vocabulary must stay consistent through the whole flow — a "Publish" button should produce a "Published" confirmation, not "Success!" or "Done."
- **Errors are precise, not apologetic.** State what happened and how to fix it, in the interface's voice — never vague ("Something went wrong") and never overly casual in a serious context ("Oops! 🙈").
- **Empty states are an invitation to act**, not just an explanation of absence: state what's missing *and* what to do about it.
- **One job per element.** A label labels. An example demonstrates. Helper text and error text never double up as marketing copy.
- **Avoid AI-generated-sounding copy patterns**: excessive em-dashes, "Unlock the power of…", triplet adjective lists ("fast, flexible, and powerful"), and generic testimonial/pricing-page boilerplate — unless the brief specifically calls for that register.

---

## 10. Execution Workflow

Work through these steps in order for every screen or component:

1. **Detect the stack** (check `package.json`, existing config/theme files) and output in the project's actual syntax — Tailwind classes, CSS-in-JS objects, SCSS, or plain CSS custom properties — don't introduce a second styling system.
2. **Complete the Mandatory Execution Protocol** (Section 1) — Context Analysis, Token Plan, Anti-Generic Validation — before writing any code.
3. **Mobile-first.** Write base styles for the smallest viewport first, then layer `sm:` / `md:` / `lg:` breakpoints upward. No design should cause horizontal scroll on any viewport ≥320px unless explicitly intended (e.g., a horizontal carousel).
4. **Theme via tokens, not hardcoded values.** Apply the token propagation rule from Section 2.3 as you write markup, not as a later pass.
5. **Build accessibility in the same pass as markup** (Section 6) — `aria-*` attributes and focus states are written alongside the elements they describe, not retrofitted.
6. **Design for edge cases from the start** (Section 7) — empty, loading, error, partial, and overflow states are part of the first implementation, not a follow-up ticket.
7. **Run the critique pass.** Take a screenshot/render if the environment allows it, apply the "remove one accessory" test (cut one decorative element that doesn't serve the brief), and confirm boldness was spent in exactly one place while everything else stays quiet and disciplined.

---

## 11. Pre-Ship Self-Review Checklist

Run every screen/component through this before considering it done:

- [ ] Would this design be visually distinguishable from the generic default for a *similar but different* brief? If not, revisit §0/§1.
- [ ] All spacing values are multiples of 4/8 (§3.2).
- [ ] No pure `#000`/`#fff`; contrast ≥4.5:1 for body text (§2.1).
- [ ] All color and type values are expressed as tokens, not hardcoded (§2.3).
- [ ] Every interactive element has hover/active/focus-visible/disabled states, ≥44×44px hit area (§4).
- [ ] Loading, empty, error, and overflow/truncation states are all designed, not just the happy path (§7).
- [ ] Icons are one consistent SVG set; no emoji-as-icon (§5).
- [ ] Copy is specific, active-voice, and free of generic AI-copy tics (§9).
- [ ] Keyboard navigation and screen-reader labeling both work end-to-end (§6).
- [ ] Exactly one "signature" bold choice exists; everything else is quiet and disciplined around it — **unless this is a pure utility interface, B2B dashboard, or data-dense table**, in which case functional clarity and information density stand in for a signature element, and this exemption has been explicitly stated rather than assumed (§1).
